newsitem.title: ITALY: Omnitel still winning admiring glances.
newsitem.headline: Omnitel still winning admiring glances.

text.p: Italy's second mobile phone group Omnitel still wins admiring glances from budding mobile players, but analysts said on Monday competition factors and Omnitel's statute would count against one of them taking a stake.

Italy's third mobile licence is set to be offered to tender early next year, and while the licence's regulations are not yet clear, talk has persisted that a potential licence applicant might find it easier to look at joining the Omnitel grouping.

Analysts say that some European experiences have suggested that it can be difficult for a competitor to enter a mobile market when full competition has existed for two to three years, but they point out Italy is still a strong growth market.

Italy's two mobile players -- state-controlled Telecom Italia Mobile (TIM) and the Omnitel consortium -- have seen rapid growth and analysts believe that there should be room for a third entrant to start up and operate profitably.

One grouping who has already stated it aims to compete for the third licence is Albacom, a joint venture between British Telecommunications and Italian state-controlled bank BNL, which has teamed up with TV and advertising group Mediaset.
However, Mediaset has often said that it has not ruled out an interest in Omnitel, while its new partner BT says Omnitel is still a possibility it has not rejected.

BT's head of European operations Pat Gallagher said at the weekend that if market conditions and regulations were unfavourable at the time of the third licence being issued then it could look at an investment in Omnitel as an alternative.
Gallagher said that Omnitel's stature forbids the control of the company to change for five years, but still added that Omnitel was a possibility that BT was studying closely.
Omnitel started operating in December and has grown rapidly backed by its big shareholders Olivetti, US groups Bell Atlantic and AirTouch, German Mannesmann and Swedish Telia.

Analysts pointed out that with such rapid growth in the mobile Italian market, competition authorities would not want to see any consolidation of the market by potential third licence players teaming up with the second player Omnitel.

Apart from Albacom/Mediaset, they pointed out that a third licence should attract interest from other consortiums such as Global One (France Telecom/Deutsche Telekom/Sprint) and also the Swiss/Spanish/Sweddish/Dutch combination Unisource.

Telecoms analyst at HSBC James Capel Paul Ryb, "Given the size of the Italian mobile phone market there is plenty of room for a third operator especially with the full liberalisation of voice telephony looming in January 1998".
He added that the regulations would need to be seen to assess the full potential of a third licence.

Mediaset, is thought to have studied the possibility of taking over Olivetti to acquire its Omnitel stake but this is considered to be too complex a process, selling off the rest of Olivetti to just get at its 35.5 percent stake in Omnitel.
"Although the Omnitel stake is valuable, taking over Olivetti would be a little too extreme," said one Milan analyst.
